item.title: UW-Madison prioritizes artificial intelligence in alumni address
item.description:
# UW-Madison prioritizes artificial intelligence in alumni address ## University of Wisconsin-Madison interim chancellor Eric Wilcots and College of Computing and Artificial Intelligence Dean Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau said universities should be stewards of AI as a public good. Interim chancellor Eric Wilcots and founding dean of University of Wisconsin-Madison’s new College of Computing and Artificial Intelligence (CAI) Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau presented a measured view of artificial intelligence in higher education at a Wisconsin Foundation and Alumni Association (WFAA) virtual panel on August 18.
![UW_now_live.png](https://snworksceo.imgix.net/car/69c824eb-84ca-451a-94d0-d0ef9615b60c.sized-1000x1000.png?w=390.625)
“[AI] is a huge opportunity to accelerate research, to accelerate innovation, to build new companies, and that's happening all around us,” Arpaci-Dusseau said.
“AI is a significant and transformative technological force,” Arpaci-Dusseau said.
He said before AI, Piazza allowed students to receive timely, accurate answers to course questions from professors and teaching assistants, and that student questions on Piazza helped instructors understand where people were getting confused.
“Because suddenly, instead of posting a question to a social network to get an answer, you can just ask ChatGPT.”
“It's a piece of software that does certain things well and certain things poorly, and we should just treat it as such… no AI agent is going to replace a really great textbook, and I feel very confident about that.”
The interdisciplinary [RISE-AI](https://www.dailycardinal.com/article/2025/11/uws-rise-ai-collaboration-introduces-ai-to-campus-wide-research), [RISE-THRIVE](https://rise.wisc.edu/rise-thrive/) and [RISE-EARTH](https://www.dailycardinal.com/article/2026/02/sustainability-hiring-initiative-announces-new-lead-headquarters) hiring initiatives aim to capitalize on that.

item.title: The Trailblazing School on the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# The Trailblazing School on the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence On a Friday morning in early March, about 100 students at Washington Leadership Academy (WLA), a public charter secondary high school in the District of Columbia, gathered in the assembly hall for a “Hackathon,” a hands-on event designed to teach students how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used in real life. The Hackathon gave the students a challenge: build a chatbot powered by AI to address real-world needs and problems.
One junior offered a more precise critique than many adults: “The term ‘artificial intelligence’ isn’t real because to be intelligent you have to be able to teach yourself.
A senior showed me a personal AI receptionist he had built on his own time that answers emails, handles phone calls, and organizes calendars, which he hopes to sell to local businesses.
Most of the school’s teachers are using AI. In a [February 2025](https://dccharters.org/blog/guest-blog-at-wla-ai-is-happening-now) survey, 85 percent reported using it professionally, with more than 80 percent doing so on a daily or weekly basis.
They input their country into a chatbot to see whether they could survive a three-year simulated war against Clarksonia, allocating its population across soldiers, scientists, artists, and educators, and selecting a key natural resource.
Niyesha Coleman, the school’s math instructional coach, built a gamified chatbot that walked students through practice problems, offering hints and feedback in a voice trained to sound like hers.
Teachers at WLA, meanwhile, are using AI to support students in ways that weren’t previously possible.
So, he created an AI tool that generated questions modeled on the few already released by the College Board.
WLA teachers are also using AI to address the day-to-day administrative challenges that plague their professional lives.
Clarkson, for example, uses AI to generate a weekly newsletter for the parents of his 86 students, something he says he would never have time to do otherwise.
AI now centralizes daily attendance data on a single dashboard, synthesized with a historical record of absences so that staff can identify and reach out to struggling students before their truancy becomes chronic.
With tools like ChatGPT, students can generate full assignments in seconds, raising questions about authorship, original thinking, and academic integrity.
Tasks focused on summary, recall, or formulaic response are often the easiest for AI to complete and may require little analysis or creativity from students if they do undertake them on their own.
With the development of AI tools that collect increasingly granular information about how students think, write, and learn, schools have been left to figure out their own guardrails for protecting student data.

item.title: A.I., Dostoevsky and the very human fear of freedom
item.description:
The rise of A.I., especially large language models (L.L.M.s) such as ChatGPT and Grok, promises convenience; they largely prove to be quite successful in fulfilling that function.
L.L.M.s are not only forms of _artificial_ intelligence, but are also an expression of _externalized_ intelligence—that is, intelligence that removes from consumers the burden of thinking, interpreting or deciding anything for themselves at all.
If Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor is a portrait of the human longing to escape the agony of freedom, then our contemporary fascination with artificial intelligence is simply its latest incarnation. The danger is not that A.I. will ever “replace” human intelligence but that we will welcome its rule and authority, finding in its artificially constructed confidence a relief from the trembling work of moral and spiritual freedom.
